blocks.text: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called its elements. In a counting problem, all objects under consideration form the universal set, written U. For any finite set A, its size (or cardinality), written n(A), is the number of elements in A. A Venn diagram shows U as a rectangle and each set inside U as a circle. When two circles A and B cross, they split the rectangle into four separate regions: elements in A only, elements in both A and B, elements in B only, and elements in neither set.

Three operations build new sets from existing ones. The intersection, written A ∩ B, contains the elements that belong to both A and B. Two sets with no elements in common have n(A ∩ B) = 0 and are called disjoint. The union, written A ∪ B, contains every element that belongs to A, to B, or to both. The complement of A, written A′, contains every element of U that is not in A, so n(A) + n(A′) = n(U). If every element of A also belongs to B, then A is called a subset of B, and the circle for A lies wholly inside the circle for B.

blocks.text: Figure 1 records how 120 members of a leisure centre used the pool (P) and the gym (G) last month. Each number counts a single region, so 34 used the pool only and 22 used both facilities, giving n(P) = 34 + 22 = 56. When two sets overlap, adding n(A) and n(B) counts every element of A ∩ B twice, once in each circle. Subtracting the overlap once gives the inclusion–exclusion rule for two sets:
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

For three sets A, B and C, adding n(A), n(B) and n(C) counts elements in two sets twice and elements in all three sets (A ∩ B ∩ C) three times. Subtracting the three pairwise overlaps removes those three-set elements three times as well, leaving them uncounted, so they are added back once:
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)

blocks.text: Many computing tasks hold items in sequence and restrict which item may be taken out next. Two standard data structures enforce opposite rules: the stack and the queue. Both store items in the order they arrive, yet they differ in where items leave.

A stack allows additions and removals at one end only, called the top, like a pile of trays. The operation push(x) places item x on the top, pop() removes and returns the item currently at the top, and peek() reads that top item without removing it. Because the most recently added item is always the first to leave, a stack follows the rule last in, first out (LIFO). If several items are pushed onto an empty stack and then all popped, they come out in exact reverse order. Editors use a stack for "undo" steps, where the latest action must be undone first.

A queue separates the two ends, like people waiting at a ticket window. The operation enqueue(x) adds item x at the back, dequeue() removes and returns the item at the front, and front() reads that front item without removing it. Because the earliest item still waiting is the first to leave, a queue follows first in, first out (FIFO) and keeps arrival order intact. Print jobs and incoming network requests wait in queues so each is handled in turn.

blocks.text: Adding the same thermal energy to equal masses of water and copper warms the copper far more than the water. This difference is captured by the specific heat capacity c of a substance: the thermal energy, in joules (J), needed to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram (kg) of that substance by 1 kelvin (K), provided no change of state such as melting or boiling occurs. Because a temperature step of 1 degree Celsius (°C) equals a step of 1 K, specific heat capacity has the same numerical value in J/(kg·K) and in J/(kg·°C). For an object of mass m whose temperature changes by ΔT = T_final − T_initial without changing state, the thermal energy Q absorbed (or released, as a magnitude) is
Q = m × c × ΔT

One kilojoule (kJ) is 1,000 J. While c belongs to the material, the product C = m × c (measured in J/K) is called the heat capacity of that particular object: how many joules are needed to warm the whole object by 1 K. Table 1 lists specific heat capacities of four substances at room temperature. Water has a remarkably high value, more than four times that of aluminium and more than ten times that of copper.

blocks.text: When a hotter object at initial temperature T₁ and a cooler object at initial temperature T₂ are placed together inside a thermally insulated container, called a calorimeter, thermal energy flows from the hotter object to the cooler one until both reach the same final equilibrium temperature T_f. If no change of state occurs and negligible heat is exchanged with the container or outside air, conservation of energy requires that the thermal energy lost by the hotter object equals the thermal energy gained by the cooler object:
m₁ × c₁ × (T₁ − T_f) = m₂ × c₂ × (T_f − T₂)
Solving this balance shows that T_f always lies between T₂ and T₁, closer to the starting temperature of whichever object has the larger heat capacity m × c.

blocks.text: How much a structural bar stretches under a pull depends on the force, on the bar’s length and thickness, and on the material. To separate geometry from material properties, engineers work with axial stress and axial strain instead of force and extension alone.

When equal and opposite forces of magnitude F pull outward along the axis of a straight bar (tension) or push inward (compression), at right angles to its cross-sectional area A, the axial stress σ is the force per unit area:
σ = F ÷ A

With F in newtons (N) and A in square metres (m²), stress is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². One megapascal (MPa) is 10⁶ Pa; because 1 m² = 10⁶ square millimetres (mm²), 1 MPa is also 1 N/mm². For a solid circular rod of radius r, the cross-sectional area is A = π × r², so doubling the radius multiplies A by four. If a bar of unloaded length L₀ changes length by ΔL, its axial strain ε is the fractional change in length:
ε = ΔL ÷ L₀

Because ΔL and L₀ carry the same length unit, those units cancel and ε has no unit. At moderate loads a material behaves elastically: it returns to L₀ when unloaded, and up to its proportional limit axial stress is proportional to axial strain (Hooke’s law, σ = E × ε). Beyond the elastic limit, unloading leaves permanent deformation. The constant E is Young’s modulus, measured in pascals or gigapascals (1 GPa = 10⁹ Pa = 1,000 MPa):
E = σ ÷ ε = (F × L₀) ÷ (A × ΔL)
Young’s modulus belongs to the material itself, not to the size or shape of the bar. Figure 1 plots σ against ε in the linear elastic region for steel and aluminium; the slope of each line is E.

blocks.text: When a firm buys a long-lived asset such as a machine or a delivery van, it does not record the whole purchase cost C as an expense in the year of purchase. Instead, accounting depreciation spreads that cost across the asset’s useful life of n years, the period over which the firm expects to use it. Depreciation allocates historical cost across accounting periods; it is not an annual cash payment and does not track day-to-day resale prices.

At the end of the n years, the firm expects to sell or scrap the asset for an estimated residual value (also called salvage value), S. The total cost to be written off over the asset’s life is its depreciable base, C − S. At any date, accumulated depreciation is the sum of all depreciation expenses recorded for the asset so far, and the asset’s book value (carrying value) is
book value = C − accumulated depreciation
Two common methods allocate the same total C − S on different schedules. The straight-line method records an equal expense in every year of useful life:
annual straight-line expense = (C − S) ÷ n

The declining-balance method is an accelerated method: it multiplies the asset’s opening book value at the start of each year by a fixed annual rate r. In the double-declining-balance version, r = 2 ÷ n, twice the straight-line rate of 1 ÷ n:
year-t expense = r × opening book value of year t (not below book value S)

Notice that S is not subtracted before multiplying by r. Instead, S serves as a floor: book value may never be reduced below S. In whichever year r × opening book value would push closing book value below S, that year’s expense is capped at opening book value − S, and any remaining years record €0. Figure 1 compares both methods for a machine with C = €80,000, S = €16,000 and n = 4 years.

blocks.text: In a market for a good, the quantity demanded, written Qd, is the amount buyers are willing and able to purchase at a given price. By the law of demand, when other influences stay the same, a higher price lowers Qd, so the demand curve slopes downwards from left to right. The quantity supplied, written Qs, is the amount sellers are willing and able to offer at a given price. By the law of supply, when other influences stay the same, a higher price raises Qs, so the supply curve slopes upwards.

Left to itself, the market settles at equilibrium, the point where the demand and supply curves cross and Qd equals Qs. The price and quantity at that crossing are the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity. At any price below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer, creating excess demand, or a shortage:
shortage = Qd − Qs (when Qd > Qs)
At any price above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, creating excess supply, or a surplus:
surplus = Qs − Qd (when Qs > Qd)
Because neither buyers nor sellers can be forced to trade, the quantity actually bought and sold at any price, when the government itself neither buys nor sells the good, is the smaller of Qd and Qs.

Governments sometimes enact price controls, legal limits on what may be charged. A price ceiling is a legal maximum price, such as a cap on housing rents. If a ceiling is set above the equilibrium price, it is non-binding: the market reaches equilibrium without breaking the law, so the ceiling has no effect unless rising demand later pushes the equilibrium price past it. If a ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, it is binding: the price cannot rise to equilibrium, so it stays at the ceiling, only Qs units are sold, and a shortage persists.

A price floor is a legal minimum price, such as a support price for farm produce. A floor set below the equilibrium price is non-binding, because the market already trades above it. A floor set above the equilibrium price is binding: the price stays at the floor, private buyers purchase only Qd units, and a surplus persists. blocks.text: An observational study watches people as they already live and records what goes with what; an experiment intervenes. In an experiment, researchers deliberately vary one factor, the independent variable (also called the explanatory variable), and measure what happens to an outcome, the dependent variable (the response variable). In a basic two-group design, the experimental group receives the active treatment being tested, while the control group is handled in the same way in every other respect except that it does not receive that active treatment. Without a control group, a change over time could come from practice, normal recovery or outside events rather than from the treatment.

Who enters each group matters just as much. If participants choose their own group, or a clinician steers keener people into the experimental group, the groups differ from the start, a flaw called selection bias. Random assignment prevents this by using a chance procedure, such as drawing lots or a random-number generator, to place each participant into a group. In large enough groups, chance spreads pre-existing differences in age, baseline skill or motivation roughly evenly between them. Random assignment is distinct from random sampling: random sampling draws participants by chance from a wider population so the sample represents that population, whereas random assignment divides whichever participants are already in the study between the groups.

Even balanced groups can diverge if people know what they are getting. When participants improve or behave differently simply because they expect a treatment to have an effect, researchers speak of the placebo effect. To match expectations across groups, the control group is often given a placebo, an inactive look-alike such as a plain starch tablet, under blinding (also called masking). In a single-blind experiment, participants do not know whether they are in the experimental or the control group, while the researchers dealing with them do. Yet researchers have expectations too: experimenter bias arises when staff unintentionally give subtle encouragement or score borderline cases more generously in one group. In a double-blind experiment, neither the participants nor the staff who deal with them or rate their outcomes know each participant's group until measurement is finished.

Together, a control group, random assignment and blinding protect internal validity: the degree to which differences in the dependent variable within the study can be attributed to the independent variable rather than to confounders, outside factors that vary alongside the treatment. High internal validity is not the same as external validity, which asks how far the result generalises to other people and everyday settings outside the trial. Nor does random assignment settle internal validity once and for all: if groups are tested under unequal conditions, or if differential attrition occurs because participants drop out of one group far more often or for different reasons than the other, the groups that finish are no longer comparable.

blocks.text: In the philosophy of science, the problem of demarcation asks what separates empirical science from non-scientific or pseudoscientific claims. An early answer held that scientific statements are those that observation can verify, meaning prove true. The philosopher Karl Popper objected that verification fails for universal statements, claims that cover every instance of a kind, such as "All swans are white." However many white swans observers record, the next swan might still be black, so finite observations never prove a universal statement true. Between verification and refutation there is a logical asymmetry: one genuine black swan is enough to refute the universal claim.

Popper therefore proposed falsifiability as the mark of empirical science. A statement or theory is falsifiable if it is capable of conflicting with possible, conceivable observations. To be falsifiable, a theory must rule out specific observable outcomes and make risky predictions, definite forecasts that could turn out false when checked. Falsifiable does not mean false: a well-established physical law is falsifiable because we can state clearly what observation would refute it if that observation ever occurred, even if every test so far agrees with the law. By contrast, a statement that allows every conceivable outcome — whether by covering both sides ("It will rain or it will not"), by using wording so vague that almost anything can be read as a hit, or by appealing to undetectable forces compatible with opposite behaviours — forbids nothing and is unfalsifiable.

When a theory survives severe attempts to refute its risky predictions, Popper says it is corroborated, not proved forever true: it has stood up to testing so far, while remaining open to future refutation. Fitting observations carries scientific weight only when those observations could conceivably have gone against the theory.

In practice, testing a theory also relies on auxiliary hypotheses, background assumptions such as that a measuring instrument is working properly or that no unknown body is disturbing the system. When an observation clashes with a prediction, the fault may lie in the main theory or in an auxiliary hypothesis. Modifying an auxiliary hypothesis stays scientific if the revised package yields new, independently testable predictions that could themselves fail. An ad hoc hypothesis, however, is an extra assumption brought in solely to explain away a failed prediction without generating any new testable consequence. Repeatedly rescuing a theory with untestable ad hoc adjustments shields it from contrary evidence and turns an initially scientific theory into unfalsifiable dogma.

blocks.text: Many chemical reactions are reversible: while reactants combine to form products (the forward reaction), products also react back to form reactants (the reverse reaction), shown by a double arrow, ⇌. In a closed vessel at constant temperature, a reversible reaction reaches chemical equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. Equilibrium is dynamic, meaning both reactions keep running at equal speeds; concentrations stop changing over time, though reactant and product concentrations need not be equal to each other.

Concentrations of gases and dissolved substances are measured in moles per litre (mol/L) and written in square brackets, such as [A]. For a balanced equation aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD involving gases or dissolved species, the equilibrium concentrations satisfy the equilibrium constant expression:

Each concentration is raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation. Pure solids, marked (s), and pure liquids, marked (l), are left out of the expression; only gases, (g), and dissolved species, (aq), enter it. At a given temperature, Kc has a single fixed value whatever starting mixture is placed in the vessel: a large value (Kc > 1) means products predominate at equilibrium, whereas a small value (Kc < 1) means reactants predominate. Substituting the concentrations of any mixture not yet known to be at equilibrium into the same fraction gives the reaction quotient, Qc:
Qc < Kc: net forward shift · Qc = Kc: at equilibrium · Qc > Kc: net reverse shift

Le Châtelier's principle describes how an equilibrium mixture responds when disturbed: it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance until Qc equals Kc again. Adding a reactant (or removing a product) at constant temperature lowers Qc below Kc, driving a net forward reaction that forms more product without changing Kc. Adding a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner without shifting equilibrium concentrations or Kc.

Temperature is the disturbance that changes Kc itself. In an endothermic reaction, which absorbs heat, heat acts like a reactant: raising the temperature shifts equilibrium towards products and increases Kc. In an exothermic reaction, which releases heat, heat acts like a product: raising the temperature shifts equilibrium towards reactants and decreases Kc.
